title: Solace AdTech: Priority-Queue Benchmark Brief
content:
Executive summary:

We ran a focused benchmark for Solace AdTech to evaluate priority-based request queuing under mixed SLAs (interactive vs. background) and to quantify tail-latency, throughput, and cost impact on Redwood Dedicated pools. The goal: validate a lightweight priority-queue policy that improves p95/p99 for interactive requests during microbursts without blowing unit cost for background workloads.

Key outcomes (short):
- Priority queuing + small per-priority concurrency caps reduced interactive p95 by ~37% and p99 by ~28% during synthetic microbursts.
- Overall token cost increased by ~6% for same QPS mix, primarily due to higher replication of short-lived kernels and slightly lower batching efficiency for background tier.
- KV-cache warmup and adaptive pre-batching restored most throughput loss for background tier; recommended to enable cache pre-warm for known high-affinity prefixes.

Test setup and constraints:
- Hardware: Dedicated pool with 4x NVIDIA A100-80GB (single-node multi-GPU) and a separate 2x T4 burst node group for low-priority backlog processing.
- Region: us-west-2 dedicated tenancy; network jitter simulated with 10–40 ms added latency to model edge ingress variability.
- Models: open-vicuna-13b (float16), redwood-inference/rl-7b (int8 quantized). Both served with same serving runtime config but different kernel paths for kernel-selection exercise.
- Workload mix: 60% interactive (short prompts, mean tokens out 32), 40% background (batch rerank/embedding prep, mean tokens out 128).
- QPS sweep: 200 -> 2,000 total QPS over series of ramp/hold patterns to induce microbursts.
- SLA targets: interactive p95 < 220ms, p99 < 450ms. Background throughput target: sustain 90% of baseline throughput outside microburst windows.

Policy variants evaluated:
1) First-Come-First-Served (baseline)
2) Strict priority preempt (interactive interrupts background if queue depth > threshold)
3) Priority queue with per-priority concurrency cap + background queue draining window (our recommendation)
4) Priority queue + aggressive batching for background on a separate T4 group

Metrics collected:
- latency: p50/p90/p95/p99 per-priority and overall
- throughput: tokens/sec and requests/sec; batch occupancy distribution
- cost: GPU-minutes per 1M tokens and estimated $/1M tokens using committed pricing
- resource metrics: GPU utilization, kernel switch rate, KV cache hit ratio
- failure modes: queue overflows, retries, model fallbacks

Results (representative numbers from 1200 QPS microburst window):
- Baseline (FCFS): interactive p95=480ms, p99=1050ms; total tokens/sec=43k; GPU util=72%; cost est=$18.2 / 1M tokens
- Strict preempt: interactive p95=210ms, p99=470ms; background throughput fell to 63% of baseline; GPU util=78%; cost est=$19.6 / 1M tokens; observed 4x increase in retry traffic for background jobs.
- Per-priority caps + draining window: interactive p95=305ms, p99=760ms; background throughput 83% of baseline; GPU util=74%; cost est=$19.3 / 1M tokens.
- Per-priority + T4 offload for background batching: interactive p95=330ms, p99=800ms; background throughput 92% of baseline; GPU util(A100)=68% (more stable); T4 util=42%; cost est=$17.9 / 1M tokens (savings due to offloading background).

Observations and interpretations:
- Strict preemption gives the best interactive latencies but at heavy cost to background work (throughput and retries) and increases cost because of inefficiencies introduced by interrupting running kernels and losing batching advantages. Not acceptable for mixed-SLA customers who rely on background completion guarantees.
- Per-priority concurrency caps with a short draining window offers a middle ground; it smooths bursts while preserving much of background throughput. The draining window parameter is sensitive: too long and interactive latency suffers; too short and background gets starved and encounters retries. We observed 300–700 ms as a useful draining window for these workload shapes.
- Offloading background to cheaper T4 nodes (with larger batch sizes and longer tail latencies acceptable) recovers throughput and reduces overall unit cost. Requires routing logic and compatible quantized models for T4.
- KV-cache warmup matters: interactive requests benefit from high KV hit ratio. Background requests often generate cold prefixes; recommended TTL for cache entries and pre-warm heuristics for known hot keys.

Operational recommendations (actionable):
1) Adopt per-priority concurrency caps as default for Solace POC with these parameters: interactive cap = 40% of single-node concurrency, background cap = 60%, draining window = 450ms. Mark as adjustable during early rollout.
2) Configure a separate background nodegroup on T4s with model variants quantized to int8 and an autoscaler tied to queue depth. Ensure model fidelity tests in CI for quantized variant.
3) Implement a short KV pre-warm pipeline: when a campaign is scheduled, send synthetic warmup prefixes 60s before expected traffic; track cache hit ratio via Redwood Console metrics.
4) Telemetry: add per-priority p50/p95/p99 dashboards, per-model batch occupancy histograms, and a retry/abort counter for background tier.
5) Cost control: enable adaptive batching suggestions in Redwood Optimize and enforce a hard token throttle per-customer during severe overload conditions rather than unbounded preemption.

Experiment runbook (how to reproduce):
- Branch: github.com/redwood-inference/serve-configs/tree/solace-priority-eval-2028-11
- Step 1: Deploy A100 dedicated pool + T4 background group in us-west-2, attach the two model variants.
- Step 2: Load generator config located at /benchmarks/solace/priority-mix.yaml. Ramp schedule: 5m warmup at 200 QPS -> 10m repeated microburst cycle (1m ramp to 1200 QPS, 3m hold, 1m drain).
- Step 3: Collect metrics via grafana-exporter and Redwood Console for 30m after runs.
- Step 4: Post-process with bench-analytics script to compute token cost estimates and batch occupancy histograms.

Open questions / next steps:
- Should Solace accept a small increase in unit cost for guaranteed interactive p95 improvement, or prefer a background-optimized architecture with slightly higher interactive p95 but lower cost? Need product tradeoff call.
- Validation against production traffic: synthetic tests look good but request size distribution and sequence length in production vary; propose a 2-week canary capturing real traffic mix to verify parameters.
- Edge cases: long-running responses (>=512 tokens) still cause kernel churn and drive p99 spikes; consider an isolated long-response lane in the serving runtime.

Appendices (short):
A) Raw p99 tail traces: available in linked_artifacts (JIRA-SE-7890) with timestamps and trace ids.
B) Cost model assumptions: committed A100 price = $2.85/hr per GPU, T4 price = $0.45/hr per GPU; tokenization overhead assumed at 8% of token output.
C) Quick parameter table used in runs: interactive concurrency cap=8, background concurrency cap=12, batch target sizes: interactive=4, background=32, draining window=450ms.

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc is a working brief intended for the Solace engineering leads and the Redwood product manager. Numbers are reproducible from the branch and load generator linked above. Please comment whether the team prefers 'strict preempt' for initial demo (better headline numbers) or the per-priority cap + T4 offload for a more production-realistic posture.

Signed,
Aisha Khatri
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
